summary: Argues that systems sharing resources over the ARPANET should use mechanisms designed for computer-to-computer communication, rather than opening Telnet connections and typing command strings as a person would. It sketches an approach to system interconnection.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 592 argues that computers should use interfaces designed for programs when they share network services. It proposes treating systems as collections of documented services and lists problems that designers would need to solve.

questions: why not use telnet between programs
why computer protocols instead of telnet simulation
why did rfc 592 discourage telnet for resource sharing
subtitle: A proposal to make network systems available as reusable computer services.

tldr.problem: The author says that using Telnet to imitate a person typing commands is suitable for experiments but not for regular computer-to-computer resource sharing.
tldr.mechanism: Systems would expose documented service modules with defined capabilities, commands and connection procedures so other systems could combine them.
tldr.outcome: The RFC outlines design issues such as connections, structured data, responsiveness, documentation, accounting, errors, parameter formats and help.

today: RFC 592 is a 1973 discussion of how network systems could expose services for use by other computers.

sections.title: From Simulated Users to Program Interfaces
sections.content: The author notes that some early resource sharing worked by having one system open a Telnet connection and generate commands as if it were a user. He considers that acceptable for experiments, but argues that real use needs mechanisms designed for communication between computers.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs sometimes used Telnet to act like people typing commands. The author argues that regular resource sharing needs interfaces built for programs to use directly.

sections.title: Systems as Network Services
sections.content:
The proposed approach treats each network system as offering service modules with advertised capabilities, documented commands and a defined connection procedure. Another system builder could use those services and integrate them into a local environment and user interface.

The RFC uses NLS Journal as an example. Its distribution, recording, cataloging and retrieval work could be separated into services that different sites provide or combine.
sections.plainLanguage: A system could make specific functions available for other programs to use. For example, journal distribution, storage, cataloging and retrieval could be offered as separate network services.

sections.title: Issues for Interconnected Systems
sections.content:
The author identifies issues that such system interconnection would need to address: connection types; translation of structured data; responsiveness; current interface documentation; accounting; error signaling across machine boundaries; standard representations for parameters; and protocol-level help.

The RFC also points to existing dialog and information systems as possible areas for combining services. It presents these ideas as a design direction that would require examples and continued discussion.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs on different systems need agreed ways to connect, exchange data, report errors and account for use. They also need clear documentation and a way to request help.
